introduction-why-good-tools-fail.core: Technically superior tools fail when they ignore human psychology: switching costs, habit, trust, perceived risk and social proof. Adoption has to be designed, as much as features do.

first_principles.problem: A faster, safer deploy tool sits unused because the old one is familiar and switching feels risky.
truths: People weigh the cost of switching heavily.

analogy.title: A better bridge nobody uses
analogy.story: Commuters keep using the old route because it's familiar and they aren't sure the new bridge leads where they need.
analogy.breaks: Some tools fail because they're genuinely worse, so validate quality first.

example.title: A tool that failed and then succeeded
flow: v2: migration script, champion teams, demos

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The same tool, a different adoption strategy.

example.outcome: adoption treated as a design problem.

check.q: Why do technically superior tools often fail to be adopted?
check.a: Habit, switching costs, perceived risk and a lack of social proof outweigh the technical advantages.

crossing-the-chasm-the-adoption-curve.core: Geoffrey Moore's lifecycle runs innovators (love new tech) → early adopters (visionaries) → early majority (pragmatists who want proof) → late majority (conservatives) → laggards. The chasm between visionaries and pragmatists is where most products die.

first_principles.problem: Early enthusiastic adoption creates false confidence, then adoption stalls at around 15%.
truths: Visionaries tolerate rough edges for advantage.
Groups don't learn from each other automatically.

analogy.title: Smartphone adoption
analogy.story: Tech enthusiasts first, but mainstream users waited for reliability, apps and friends' recommendations.
analogy.breaks: Internal populations are smaller and more connected than markets, so word of mouth matters even more.

example.title: Platform adoption stalling
flow: Diagnosis: no migration path, sparse docs
example.outcome: you can predict where adoption stalls.

check.q: What do early-majority pragmatists need before adopting?
check.a: Proven, complete solutions with references from peers similar to them.

strategies-to-cross-the-chasm.core: Cross the chasm by focusing on one beachhead segment (one service type or team cluster), delivering a 'whole product' (docs, migration tools, support, integrations), building peer references and reducing switching costs to near zero.

first_principles.problem: A platform tries to serve every team at once and fully satisfies none of the pragmatists.
truths: Success in one segment spreads to adjacent ones.
derivation: Deliver the **whole product**: docs, migration scripts, support, observability.

analogy.title: D-Day's beachhead
analogy.story: Concentrate forces on one beach, secure it, then advance inland.
analogy.breaks: Choosing too narrow a beachhead can limit impact, so pick one that leads somewhere.

example.title: A beachhead strategy
flow: Beachhead: stateless HTTP services (60% of fleet)
Whole product: codemod + runbooks + office hours
Then expand to workers, then stateful
example.outcome: adoption moves past the early adopters.

check.q: What is a 'whole product' in crossing-the-chasm terms?
check.a: The complete solution pragmatists need: not just the core tool but docs, migration support, integrations and help.

shadow-it-enemy-or-signal.core: Shadow IT (tools teams adopt without approval, like personal SaaS accounts, unsanctioned cloud resources or homegrown scripts) usually signals unmet needs or friction in the official path. Treat it as user research before enforcement.

first_principles.problem: Security discovers 40 unapproved SaaS tools and bans them, and teams find new workarounds.
derivation: **Discover** shadow IT (SSO logs, expense reports, cloud scans).
**Absorb or replace** with a better sanctioned path.

analogy.title: Desire paths across a lawn
analogy.story: Worn paths show where people actually want to walk, so smart planners pave them.
analogy.breaks: Some shadow IT is dangerous (customer data in personal tools) and needs immediate action.

example.title: Shadow CI discovered
flow: Team runs CircleCI on a personal card

check.q: What does shadow IT often indicate about a platform?
check.a: That the official tools have friction or gaps that fail to meet teams' real needs.

handling-shadow-it-pave-the-path.core: Don't punish, absorb: make the compliant path so easy and good that shadow alternatives lose their appeal. Bring popular tools in officially (with SSO, security review and billing), and offer migration help for risky ones.

first_principles.problem: Enforcement-only approaches create cat-and-mouse games and resentment.
truths: Official support adds safety and cost control.
derivation: **Replace** risky ones with better sanctioned options.
**Reduce friction** in the official path continuously.

analogy.title: Legalising and regulating a popular street market
analogy.story: Instead of chasing vendors, provide licensed stalls with safety standards, and everyone benefits.
analogy.breaks: Officialising everything creates sprawl, so consolidate where possible.

example.title: Absorbing a popular tool
flow: Teams migrate into the managed workspace

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Risk drops and users are happy.

check.q: What does 'pave the path' mean for shadow IT?
check.a: Making the sanctioned path so easy and capable that shadow alternatives are no longer needed.
